note: The 0.3.1 release PR failed both matrix legs on test_the_lint_line_goes_red_on_a_missing_gate. The test monkeypatched LINT_MODULES to ('ruff', 'nestor_no_such_lint_module') and asserted the exact substring 'MISSING nestor_no_such_lint_module'. CI's test job installs `.[keys] pytest coverage` -- the lint tools live in the lint job, deliberately -- so ruff is genuinely absent there and the probe correctly reported 'MISSING ruff, nestor_no_such_lint_module'. The check was right; the test had the contents of one venv baked into it as a fact. Reproduced locally by pointing _venv_python at a ruff-less interpreter: the old pair fails both assertions, the new pair passes both.

decisions.question: How does a test for a readiness check avoid depending on what happens to be ready?
decisions.commitment: The present half of the pair is stdlib. LINT_MODULES is monkeypatched to ('json', 'nestor_no_such_lint_module'): json imports in any interpreter that can run the probe at all, so 'MISSING <fake>' is exact and 'the importable one is not accused' holds everywhere -- the repo venv, CI's test job, a bare checkout. Nothing about the assertion depends on an install.
decisions.why: The test exists to prove the line can report un-ready. Naming a real lint tool as the control made the proof conditional on that tool being installed, which is the one thing a readiness check must not assume about its own test environment. A stdlib module is the only choice with no install story at all.

decisions.question: Is this a one-off, or a pattern?
decisions.commitment: A pattern, and this is its third instance on this branch. 0125: scripts/hook_guard.py inherited the developer's review receipt, so the write gate's deny case flipped depending on what the operator had done in the last thirty minutes. 0127: every store fixture was built by `nestor demo` or memory_init(), both of which set WAL at creation, so a read-only claim passed while being false for any store that was not already WAL. 0128: the fixtures passed an explicit --db outside the default path, so `nestor demo`'s diversion never triggered under test. Now this: the control module was one the local venv happened to carry.
decisions.why: Each time the suite agreed with the code because both were shaped by the same ambient state, and each time the defect surfaced somewhere that state differed -- a live receipt, a non-WAL store, the real default path, a CI job with a narrower install. Writing it down as a class is worth more than four separate fixes: the question to ask of any new test is not 'does this pass' but 'what in my environment is this quietly asserting'.

decisions.question: Did waiting for CI before merging the release earn its cost?
decisions.commitment: Yes, and not for the reason expected. The wait was justified on the 3.10 leg -- tests/test_version.py had broken that leg once before by importing tomllib, and this branch adds a test to that same file. 3.10 was fine. What actually failed was a test-job/dev-venv difference that both legs shared and that no amount of local running on 3.11 would have surfaced.
decisions.why: The tag is the trigger and a version number is the one part of a release nobody can correct afterwards (docs/releasing.md). Merging on green-locally would have put a failing suite on master under a v0.3.1 tag, and the fix would then have had to be 0.3.2 rather than one more commit on an unmerged branch. The cost of waiting was a few minutes; the cost of not waiting was a burnt version number.
